The doubt of future foes exiles my present joy, And wit me warns to shun such snares as threaten mine annoy; For falsehood now doth flow, and subjects’ faith doth ebb, Which should not be if reason ruled or wisdom weaved the web. But clouds of joys untried do cloak aspiring minds, Which turn to rain of late repent by changed course of winds. The top of hope supposed the root upreared shall be, And fruitless all their grafted guile, as shortly ye shall see. The dazzled eyes with pride, which great ambition blinds, Shall be unsealed by worthy wights whose foresight falsehood finds. The daughter of debate that discord aye doth sow Shall reap no gain where former rule still peace hath taught to know. My rusty sword through rest shall first his edge employ To poll their tops that seek such change or gape for future joy.

---

**The Doubt of Future Foes**

The fear of foes to come has driven out my present peace,
And prudence bids me guard against the snares that never cease;
For falsehood now abounds, while loyal faith runs dry—
A state that ne'er would be, did reason rule or wisdom guide.

Yet clouds of untried hopes still veil ambition's eager eyes,
Which soon shall turn to rain of late regret, when fortune's wind shall rise.
What seems the height of hope shall find its roots torn from the ground,
And all their cultivated schemes shall prove but barren, hollow sound.

Those eyes now dazzled by pride, by vaulting ambition blind,
Shall soon be opened wide by those whose wisdom falsehood finds.
That daughter of discord, who ever sows dissent and strife,
Shall reap no harvest here, where settled rule has taught us peace and life.

No exile, banished from abroad, shall find safe harbor in this land;
Our realm gives no shelter to sedition—let them seek some other strand.
My sword, though long at rest, shall first be roused to prove its blade,
And strike down those who crave such change or dream of triumphs yet unmade.

Anxiety over enemies yet to come robs me of the happiness I now enjoy, and my own judgment cautions me to avoid the traps that threaten to harm me. Yet ambitious hearts conceal themselves behind clouds of untested hopes, hopes that will eventually turn to storms of regret once fortune's winds shift direction. My sword, though long idle, will be the first weapon drawn to cut down anyone who seeks upheaval or yearns for a different future.
outputs.L3:
# On Present Happiness and Future Vigilance

Though I find myself in a moment of contentment, I cannot allow this happiness to blind me to the shadows gathering at the edges of my vision. The specter of future enemies looms even now, and it would be folly to mistake present peace for permanent security. This awareness compels me toward caution—a deliberate wariness against any scheme, however tempting, that might jeopardize what stability we currently enjoy. Happiness untempered by vigilance is merely happiness deferred to disaster.

This caution is not born of mere paranoia but of sober observation. I have watched with growing concern as falsehood spreads unchecked through the realm, and loyalty—once the bedrock of good governance—erodes among those I would call subjects. This decline is more than a moral failing; it is a symptom of a deeper malady. Where reason and wisdom once guided the affairs of state, I now perceive only confusion and self-interest. A government cannot long endure when the very foundations of trust and rational counsel have been so thoroughly undermined.

Yet I take some comfort in a truth that history has proven again and again: those minds consumed by ambition, who nurture untested and inflated hopes of glory, inevitably meet with disappointment. They build their castles upon foundations of pride and speculation, never pausing to consider that circumstances shift, that fortune favors no one indefinitely. When the tide turns against them—as it always does against those who overreach—they will find only regret where they once envisioned triumph. Their schemes, however elaborately conceived, cannot withstand the scrutiny of time.

Indeed, I am confident that such prideful and ambitious plots, no matter how carefully concealed, will not escape detection forever. There exist among us those of genuine perception and worth—individuals whose wisdom cuts through deception and whose loyalty remains uncorrupted. These are the ones who will uncover the deceit lurking beneath ambition's polished surface, exposing conspiracies before they can fully take root. Truth, in the end, has a way of revealing itself to those wise enough to seek it.

Let it be known, then, with absolute clarity: I will not tolerate threats from beyond our borders, nor will I suffer seditious forces to fester within them. Should the need arise, I am prepared to draw forth even a rusty sword—one perhaps dulled by disuse, but no less capable of serving justice—to suppress those who would seek disruptive and destructive change. This is not a threat issued lightly, but a solemn vow: peace will be defended, order will be maintained, and those who conspire against the common good will find no refuge from the consequences of their actions.
outputs.L4:
# The Doubt of Future Foes: A Sovereign's Meditation on Treachery and Rule

The poem attributed to Elizabeth I, often known by the title "The Doubt of Future Foes," emerges from a period of profound political tension in Tudor England, when the queen faced constant threats to her throne from both domestic conspirators and foreign powers seeking to destabilize her reign. Through carefully wrought poetic language, the speaker—understood to be the queen herself—grapples with the ever-present anxiety that accompanies political power, particularly the gnawing fear that those closest to the throne might harbor treacherous intentions beneath a mask of loyalty.

The poem's central rhetorical strategy relies heavily on extended natural metaphors, particularly imagery drawn from meteorological phenomena. Clouds gathering on the horizon represent the subtle, often imperceptible beginnings of conspiracy and dissent. Storms symbolize the eventual eruption of these plots into open rebellion or crisis, suggesting that political treachery, like weather patterns, follows a recognizable trajectory from quiet inception to violent manifestation. This use of natural imagery serves a dual purpose: it universalizes the political anxieties of the Elizabethan court by connecting them to timeless, recognizable natural cycles, while also suggesting that such threats, however alarming, are ultimately as predictable and, in some sense, as manageable as the weather itself to a prepared and vigilant ruler.

Central to the poem's thematic concerns is the persistent warning against deceptive appearances—the idea that ambition and treachery often disguise themselves in the garments of loyalty and service. The speaker cautions that those who harbor disruptive or self-serving intentions frequently present a false face to the world, concealing their true purposes until the moment is ripe for betrayal. This theme of appearance versus reality reflects broader Renaissance anxieties about the instability of truth in courtly settings, where flattery, dissimulation, and political maneuvering were considered constant dangers to a monarch's security.

The poem further addresses the specific threat of foreign-inspired sedition, alluding to the very real historical circumstances of Elizabeth's reign, in which Catholic powers on the continent, along with domestic sympathizers, sought to undermine her Protestant rule and replace her with a more religiously compliant monarch. This concern with external interference intertwines with the poem's broader meditation on loyalty, suggesting that true allegiance to the crown must be distinguished from schemes hatched abroad and imported into the realm through treacherous intermediaries.

Despite these pervasive anxieties, the poem ultimately strikes a confident and assertive tone regarding the fate of such conspiracies. The speaker declares with conviction that deceitful plots, however cunningly devised, are destined to fail. This assurance stems not from naive optimism but from a a firm belief in the fundamental strength of legitimate authority and established order. The poem suggests that loyalty—true, unwavering loyalty to the rightful sovereign—possesses an inherent power that will ultimately triumph over the corrosive effects of ambition and treachery.

Finally, the poem positions the ruler not as a passive victim of potential conspiracy but as an active, vigilant defender of the realm. The speaker's tone conveys readiness and resolve, indicating a monarch fully prepared to confront and suppress any who would seek to disrupt the established order through rebellion or foreign-backed intrigue. This closing assertion of strength and preparedness transforms the poem from a mere expression of anxiety into a declaration of sovereign power, reinforcing the image of a ruler who, despite acknowledging the very real dangers surrounding her throne, remains steadfast, watchful, and ultimately confident in her capacity to preserve both her rule and the stability of her kingdom against all who would seek its ruin.
outputs.L5:
# The Power of Small Words

We often overlook them. **The**, **and**, **for** — three tiny words that rarely draw attention to themselves, yet without them, language would collapse into chaos.

**The** is perhaps the most unassuming word in the English language, and yet it is also the most frequently used. It points, it specifies, it turns something vague into something definite. "A book" is any book; "the book" is *the* book — the one we mean, the one that matters right now. This small article carries the weight of context, memory, and shared understanding between speaker and listener.

**And** is the great connector. It links ideas, joins sentences, and builds bridges between thoughts that might otherwise stand alone. It is humble, but without it, we would be left with fragments — isolated statements unable to grow into stories, arguments, or reflections. "And" is the word of accumulation, of more, of continuation. It says: there is still something to add.

**For** carries purpose. It points toward reason, toward intention, toward the *why* behind an action. "I did it for you." "This is for tomorrow." In just three letters, it transforms an action into a gift, a plan into a promise, a moment into something directed toward the future or toward another person.

Together, these three words seem almost invisible in the flow of everyday speech. We rarely pause to consider them, for they do their work quietly, in the background, holding sentences together like the mortar between bricks. Yet if we removed them, the walls of language would fall.

Perhaps this is the quiet lesson these words offer: greatness does not always announce itself. Sometimes, it is found in the small, steady presence of things that connect, define, and give purpose — the same way *the*, *and*, and *for* connect, define, and give purpose to everything we say.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Elizabeth I's "The Doubt of Future Foes," using archaic English and themes of political betrayal and sovereignty.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Perils That Beset a Crown**

The dread of hidden knives doth chase the peace from out my breast,
And treason's whispering tongue disturbs the throne where I would rest.
The smiling face that bows full low oft hides a viper's sting,
And they who kneel before my feet may plot to slay the king.

No armor wrought of steel can guard so well as watchful mind,
For foes that walk in daylight's cloak are hardest so to find.
The seed of discord, sown by those who envy sovereign might,
Doth spring in secret, hid from sun, yet blooms in dead of night.

Let fortune's wheel turn as it will, I shall not bow to fear,
Though serpents nest within the court and falsehood draweth near.
My right is stamped by heaven's hand, no mortal plot can stay
The course that Providence hath set, come what may come this day.

Yet wisdom bids me keep mine eyes upon the shifting tide,
For trust too soon bestowed hath oft brought low both crown and pride.
The wolf that wears the shepherd's guise shall find no shelter here—
My realm is girded round with law, my scepter held with care.

So let the plotters weave their web of falsehood and of spite,
Their treach'rous threads shall snap at last beneath the weight of right.
For I was set upon this throne not by the voice of men,
But by that Power whose judgment stands beyond the reach of pen.

Thus though the doubt of future foes may cloud my present hour,
My steadfast heart shall not be moved, nor bowed by traitor's power.
The crown I wear is not mine own to cast at fortune's feet—
'Tis trust from God and from my realm, a burden and a seat.

counterfactuals.output:
# A Queen's Admonition Against Sedition

Hearken, ye subjects, to your sovereign's voice,
Who speaks not out of fear, but righteous care,
For treason creepeth where the false rejoice,
And whispers rise like poison in the air.

I did not seize this crown by wicked art,
Nor climbed I up by any traitor's stair,
God's hand alone did set me thus apart,
To rule this realm and for this realm to bear.

Let those who plot in shadow'd rooms take heed—
The throne is not a prize for grasping hands,
Nor loyalty a coin for those in need,
To spend or hoard as private gain demands.

I know the serpent's tongue, the smiling face,
That speaks fair words while daggers lie beneath,
I know how ambition wears the mask of grace,
And how disloyalty doth hide in false belief.

Yet mark me well, ye who would test my throne:
A queen forewarned is armored in her right,
I hold no malice for the truth alone,
But traitors' schemes shall crumble in the light.

To those who serve me true, my love is vast,
As mother to her children, so am I,
But those who scheme to see my kingdom cast
In chaos's hands—by justice they shall die.

Let history record: no tyrant's hand
Did guide this scepter, nor did fear compel
My rule—but duty to my native land,
And love for those I govern, guard, and shield.

So let the disaffected mark this rhyme:
Rebellion's fruit is bitter, swift, and brief,
While loyalty outlives the reach of time,
And treason ends but in the traitor's grief.

God save the realm, and those who keep it whole,
God curse the hand that seeks its bright decay,
For I shall guard this kingdom with my soul,
Till death alone shall take my crown away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem imitating Elizabethan poetic style, filled with metaphors of storms, seeds, and hidden ambition, addressing political rivals.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Rivals Who Whisper 'Neath the Common Wind

Mark how the tempest gathers in the west,
Where thunder-clouds do hoard their secret rain,
So thou, false friend, with courtesy possess'd,
Dost harbor storms beneath thy smiling reign.

Thy words are seeds cast fair upon the field,
Yet each doth hide a canker in its core;
Thou sow'st sweet promise but dost reap the yield
Of discord, hungry for ambition's store.

I know thee, schemer, though thou wear'st the guise
Of humble service to the common good—
Beneath thy bow, behind thy modest eyes,
There stirs the sap of an usurping wood.

The seed of thy intent, once buried deep,
Doth wait but for the season to unfold;
Thou tend'st it in the dark whilst others sleep,
And dream'st thyself a prince before thou'rt old.

Yet mark—the storm that thou wouldst raise to power
May turn upon the hand that bids it rise;
The seed that groweth wild in secret hour
Oft strangles him who plants it in disguise.

For I have weathered tempests of mine own,
And know the tricks of lightning dressed as light;
Thy ambition, though in modesty it's sown,
Reveals its thunder in the noonday bright.

Go, plant thy schemes in some more fertile ground
Where honest men mistake the wolf for lamb—
But here thy hidden storms shall make no sound,
For I do know the tempest that thou am.

So rage, false wind, and gather what thou wilt,
Thy harvest shall be but the chaff of shame;
For treachery, however finely built,
Doth reap at last dishonor for its name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# On the Fickle Tides of Fortune

The doubt of future woes
Exiles my present joy,
And wit me warns to shun such snares
As threaten mine annoy;
For falsehood now doth flow,
And subjects' faith doth ebb,
Which should not be if reason ruled
Or wisdom weaved the web.

But clouds of joy untried
Do cloak aspiring minds,
Which turn to rain of late repent
By course of changed winds.
The top of hope supposed
The root of rue shall be,
And fruitless all their grafted guile
As shortly ye shall see.

The dazzled eyes with pride,
The wisest wits may blind;
And fortune's wheel by vain deceit
Doth turn to their own mind.
The stately seat of one
Shall foreign scions plant,
Whom seely broods and secret plots
May thrust from what they want.

No foresight can prevent
What fate hath firmly set,
Nor mortal skill escape the net
Which subtle craft doth fret.
My reason to my rule,
My rule to reason's frame,
Have made me now to see the plots
That aim at my good name.

Let them elsewhere resort
Their practicse to pursue,
And let them know their bootless drift
But breeds their own review.
The daughter of debate,
That eke discord doth sow,
Shall reap no gain where former rule
Hath taught still peace to grow.

No foreign banished wight
Shall anchor in this port;
Our realm it brooks no strangers' force,
Let them elsewhere resort.
My rusty sword through rest
Shall first his edge employ
To poll their tops that seek such change
Or gape for future joy.

---

*[Note: This is an original composition modeled on Elizabeth I's poem, preserving its meter, rhyme structure, and allusions to Mary Queen of Scots as "the daughter of debate." It is not a discovery of a lost text but a creative emulation.]*
